title.en: Splitting Exception Groups and Adding Notes

description.en: Use ExceptionGroup.split to divide errors into retryable and fatal piles while keeping the nesting, and add_note to attach context to an error without wrapping it.

story_variants.en:
## Splitting Groups And Adding Context

"Catching by type is one way to treat a group," Vaathiyaar says. "Sometimes you want the *pieces* instead: 'give me the timeouts so I can retry them, and the rest so I can report them.' That is what `split` does -- and `add_note` lets you attach context to an error without wrapping it."

### `split` And `subgroup`

```python
group = ExceptionGroup("net", [TimeoutError("a"), ConnectionError("b"),
         ExceptionGroup("inner", [TimeoutError("c"), ValueError("d")])])
timeouts, rest = group.split(TimeoutError)
```

`split` returns a pair of groups: the members that match, and the members that don't. Both **keep the nested shape and the message** of the original (`timeouts` still has an `inner` group inside, now holding just `c`). If one side is empty it is `None`, not an empty group. `group.subgroup(KeyError)` returns only the matching half -- here `None`, since nothing is a KeyError. You can pass an exception type or a function that takes an exception and returns True/False.

For this example, `timeouts` holds the leaves `a` and `c` and `rest` holds `b` and `d`.

### Notes: Context Without Wrapping

`exc.add_note("line 3: 'abc'")` appends a string to a list called `exc.__notes__`, and the notes are printed under the traceback. The exception keeps its type and message, so callers that catch `ValueError` still work. That is the point: you can say *where* it failed on the way up, and then plain `raise` it again.

> **Vaathiyaar's caveat:** notes are just a list of strings on the object. They are shown in tracebacks, but `str(exc)` does not include them, so do not parse them for logic -- use them for humans.

Today you split a nested group by retryability, then annotate a parse error and re-raise it.

under_the_hood.summary: split and subgroup copy the tree of an exception group into matching and non-matching halves, while add_note simply appends strings to a list on the exception that the traceback printer shows below the error.

steps.title: split walks the whole tree
steps.body: `group.split(cond)` visits every leaf, checking the condition (an exception type, a tuple of types, or a function). It returns two groups, each with the original message and the original nesting, but only the leaves that did (or did not) match.

left.label: Original
left.code:
net
  TimeoutError a
  ConnectionError b
  inner
    TimeoutError c
    ValueError d

right.label: split(TimeoutError)
right.code:
match: net
  a
  inner
    c
rest: net
  b
  inner
    d

steps.title: Empty sides are None
steps.body: If no leaf lands on one side, that side is `None` rather than an empty group, because a group may never be empty. `subgroup(cond)` returns just the matching half, or `None`. Check before using: `if timeouts is not None:`.

steps.title: Counting leaves needs recursion
steps.body: `len(group.exceptions)` counts only the top-level members, and a nested group counts as one. To count real errors, recurse: a member that is a `BaseExceptionGroup` contributes the count of its own members, anything else counts as 1.

stepDescriptions.description: Is this member itself a group?
Yes: add up the leaves inside it.
No: it is a single error, count 1.

steps.title: add_note appends to __notes__
steps.body: `exc.add_note(text)` requires a string and appends it to `exc.__notes__`, creating the list on first use. Nothing else about the exception changes: its type, arguments and `str()` stay the same. The traceback printer then shows each note on its own line below the error message.

lines: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'

steps.title: Re-raise with a bare raise
steps.body: The usual pattern is `except ValueError as exc: exc.add_note(...); raise`. A bare `raise` re-raises the same object, so the original traceback is kept and callers can still catch the original type. Notes also work on groups, and on every leaf you reach.

under_the_hood.takeaway: split divides a group by a rule while keeping its shape; add_note adds human context without changing the exception. Check for None, count leaves recursively, and use a bare raise.
